Clinical Reference

COPD Exacerbation (v2)

On this page
An acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, sputum volume/purulence) over ≤14 days in a patient with COPD, driven by amplified airway inflammation — usually a viral or bacterial trigger — that demands intensified bronchodilation, a short steroid course, and correction of gas exchange.
GOLD 2025 · Rome severity O₂ target SpO₂ 88–92% Prednisone 40 mg × 5 d (REDUCE) NIV for pH <7.35 + PaCO₂ >45 In-hospital mortality ~4–10% (up to ~25% if ICU)
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story from trigger to hypercapnia

COPD is a disease of chronically obstructed expiratory airflow from a mix of small-airway disease (inflamed, narrowed, mucus-plugged bronchioles) and emphysema (destroyed alveolar walls → lost elastic recoil and lost tethering that normally holds airways open). Baseline, the patient copes. An exacerbation is what happens when a trigger — most often a virus (rhinovirus leads), a bacterium (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis; Pseudomonas in advanced disease), or a pollution/cold-air insult — pours petrol on that smouldering airway inflammation.

The trigger amplifies neutrophilic (and sometimes eosinophilic) inflammation → mucosal edema, bronchospasm, and mucus hypersecretion. Airways narrow further and empty even more slowly. Because the patient cannot fully exhale before the next breath begins, air stacks up — dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP). Hyperinflation flattens the diaphragm, putting it at a mechanical disadvantage, so the work of breathing skyrockets just as the muscles are least efficient. Meanwhile ventilation and perfusion fall out of register (V/Q mismatch) → hypoxemia; and as the fatiguing respiratory pump fails to move enough air, CO₂ accumulates → respiratory acidosis (hypercapnic respiratory failure). That pH is the number that decides whether they get a BiPAP mask or a tube.

Breathing in COPD is like trying to run while breathing through a floppy straw that collapses on exhale. During an exacerbation the straw clogs and kinks: each breath in is easy enough, but you can't get the air out before you need the next one. Air piles up (hyperinflation), the "bellows" (diaphragm) is stretched flat and can't pull, and you tire out — first the oxygen drops, then the CO₂ climbs and the blood turns acidic.

The exacerbation cascade and where each therapy interrupts it — the through-line of this whole guide. Adapts to light/dark theme.
Gross lung, severe bullous emphysema: alveolar walls destroyed into large air-filled bullae — the lost recoil and tethering that make airways collapse on exhale.
Yale Rosen, CC BY-SA 2.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Histology (10×): abnormally enlarged airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with alveolar-wall destruction — the microscopic basis of hyperinflation.
Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Every drug in this guide maps onto one arrow in the cascade above. SABA (β₂-agonist) relaxes airway smooth muscle; SAMA (antimuscarinic) blocks vagal bronchoconstriction and secretions — together they widen the straw so trapped air can escape. Systemic corticosteroids switch off the transcription of inflammatory cytokines, shrinking mucosal edema over 24–48 h. Antibiotics remove a bacterial trigger when the sputum turns purulent. Controlled oxygen corrects hypoxemia without abolishing hypoxic drive, and NIV mechanically unloads the fatiguing pump and blows off CO₂.

🗂️

Defining & grading — the four frameworks you actually use

Diagnosis of COPD itself requires a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 on spirometry. Once diagnosed, four different classifications answer four different questions.

1 · Airflow severity — GOLD spirometric grade (FEV₁ % predicted)

GradeFEV₁ (% predicted, post-BD)Label
GOLD 1≥ 80%Mild
GOLD 250–79%Moderate
GOLD 330–49%Severe
GOLD 4< 30%Very severe

2 · Symptom / exacerbation burden — GOLD "ABE" groups (drives chronic inhalers)

GroupExacerbations (past year)Symptoms (mMRC / CAT)Initial inhaler
A0–1 (no hospitalization)Low (mMRC 0–1 / CAT <10)A bronchodilator
B0–1 (no hospitalization)High (mMRC ≥2 / CAT ≥10)LABA + LAMA
E≥2 moderate or ≥1 hospitalizationAnyLABA + LAMA (add ICS if eos ≥300)

GOLD 2023 merged the old C and D groups into a single high-risk "E" group — the exacerbation history, not the symptom score, is what puts a patient there.

3 · Exacerbation severity — GOLD 2025 / Rome proposal

SeverityDefining featuresSetting
MildDyspnea VAS <5, RR <24, HR <95, SpO₂ ≥92% on room air (or usual), CRP <10 mg/LHome; ↑ short-acting bronchodilators
Moderate≥3 of: dyspnea VAS ≥5, RR ≥24, HR ≥95, SpO₂ <92%, CRP ≥10 — but no hypercapnic acidosisOften needs steroids ± antibiotics; may admit
SevereHypercapnia with acidosis: PaCO₂ >45 mmHg and pH ≤7.35 (± hypoxemia)Hospital; consider NIV / ICU

The Rome criteria (2021) formalized severity by physiology and biomarkers rather than by how much treatment was given — a deliberate move away from the old "mild = extra inhaler / severe = hospital" circular definition.

4 · Symptom pattern for antibiotics — Anthonisen criteria

Cardinal symptomTypeAntibiotic benefit
① ↑ Dyspnea  ② ↑ Sputum volume  ③ ↑ Sputum purulenceType 1 = all 3Yes — clear benefit
Any 2 of the 3Type 2Yes if purulence is one of them
1 of 3 (± URI, fever, wheeze)Type 3Usually no
Sputum purulence (colour change) is the single best bedside predictor of a bacterial cause and antibiotic benefit — a green/yellow sample matters more than volume alone.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Read each finding as evidence of one of two problems: increased airflow obstruction / air trapping (dyspnea, wheeze, accessory-muscle use) or failing gas exchange (cyanosis, confusion, asterixis). The second group is what escalates care.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Increased dyspnea~100%The defining symptom — narrowed airways + dynamic hyperinflation raise the work of breathing; the flattened diaphragm can't compensate.
Cough~85%Airway inflammation and mucus stimulate cough receptors; often the earliest sign of a brewing exacerbation.
Increased sputum volume~60%Goblet-cell/submucosal-gland hypersecretion driven by the inflammatory trigger.
Sputum purulence (colour change)~50–60%Neutrophil myeloperoxidase turns sputum green/yellow — the marker that most predicts a bacterial cause.
Wheeze / prolonged expiration~50%Turbulent flow through narrowed, bronchospastic airways; a long expiratory phase reflects air trapping.
Accessory-muscle use / pursed-lip breathing~45%Recruiting sternocleidomastoids/scalenes when the diaphragm fails; pursed lips create auto-PEEP to splint airways open.
Tachypnea (RR ≥24)~45%Chemoreceptor drive from hypoxemia/hypercapnia; a rising RR precedes decompensation.
Tachycardia (HR ≥95)~35%Sympathetic drive, hypoxemia, and β-agonist effect; new AF is common and worsens prognosis.
Hypoxemia (SpO₂ <92%)~30%V/Q mismatch from mucus plugging and regional collapse.
Cyanosis<15%≥5 g/dL deoxygenated hemoglobin — a late, severe-hypoxemia sign.
Confusion / drowsiness / asterixis<15%CO₂ narcosis — rising PaCO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier, lowering CSF pH. A hard flag for NIV/ICU.
Peripheral edema (new/worse)<15%Cor pulmonale: chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → right-heart strain.
Read the patternWheeze, accessory-muscle use and a long expiratory phase say "obstruction/trapping" — treat with bronchodilators and steroids. Cyanosis, confusion, asterixis and a silent chest say "gas exchange is failing" — check an ABG and think NIV/ICU now.

🩻

Imaging — what to order, the trigger, and the key finding

StudyWhen / threshold to orderKey finding & why it matters
Chest X-ray (PA/lateral)Essentially every hospitalized exacerbationHyperinflation (>10 posterior ribs, flat diaphragms, increased retrosternal air), narrow "tear-drop" heart. Its main job is to rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion, and pulmonary edema that mimic or complicate an exacerbation.
CT chestIf PE suspected (CT-PE), for bullae/complication clarification, or discordant pictureQuantifies emphysema, detects bullae/pneumothorax and, with contrast, PE — a common and under-diagnosed exacerbation mimic.
Bedside lung ultrasoundRapid triage of dyspnea at the bedsideA-lines + lung sliding argue for COPD; B-lines/effusion point toward cardiogenic pulmonary edema instead.
ECGAll — screen for arrhythmia/ischemiaSinus tachycardia, multifocal atrial tachycardia, new AF, right-heart strain (P-pulmonale, RBBB, RAD).
COPD exacerbation CXR: hyperinflated lung fields, flattened hemidiaphragms and a long, narrow cardiac silhouette. First job — exclude pneumonia/pneumothorax.
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0 — Wikimedia Commons
CT chest: extensive low-attenuation areas of emphysema (here basal-predominant, α₁-antitrypsin pattern) — destroyed parenchyma with no visible walls.
Fregonese & Stolk, CC BY 2.0 — Wikimedia Commons
"Barrel chest": an increased anteroposterior diameter from chronic hyperinflation — a bedside clue to the underlying COPD.
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
🧪

Interpreting the labs — direction, mechanism, and confounders

TestTypical moveWhy it moves · confounders / false readings
ABG — pH↓ (<7.35)Acute respiratory acidosis from CO₂ retention. pH is the master triage number: ≤7.35 with ↑CO₂ → NIV; falling toward <7.25 despite NIV → intubation.
ABG — PaCO₂↑ (>45)Alveolar hypoventilation from a fatiguing pump + dead-space. Beware the chronic retainer: a high CO₂ with a normal pH and high bicarbonate is compensated baseline, not acute failure.
ABG/serum HCO₃⁻↑ (chronic)Renal metabolic compensation for chronic hypercapnia. A high baseline bicarbonate tells you this is a chronic retainer — interpret today's gas against it.
PaO₂ / SpO₂↓V/Q mismatch. Over-oxygenation is dangerous here (see O₂ target) — chase 88–92%, not 100%.
Blood eosinophilsVariableBiomarker of corticosteroid-responsive inflammation. Eosinopenia (<0.05 ×10⁹/L) is a marker of a worse acute prognosis (the "E" in DECAF); a high count predicts steroid responsiveness and shorter stay.
CRP↑Supports an inflammatory/infective exacerbation; helps grade Rome severity and (with purulence) supports antibiotics.
ProcalcitoninLow → hold abxA low PCT can support withholding/stopping antibiotics, but GOLD advises it be used cautiously — clinical picture (purulence, Anthonisen) still leads.
CBC — WBC↑Infection or the leukocytosis of systemic corticosteroids (demargination) — don't over-read a modest bump on steroids.
BNP / NT-proBNPUse to sortA low value argues against concomitant heart failure when the dyspnea cause is ambiguous.
TroponinMay ↑Demand ischemia / right-heart strain; a rise flags higher mortality and warrants an ACS work-up if the story fits.
Glucose↑ on treatmentSystemic steroids drive hyperglycemia — check and cover, especially in diabetics.
Sputum Gram stain/culture—Reserve for treatment failure, frequent exacerbators, or Pseudomonas risk (advanced disease, recent abx/hospitalization, bronchiectasis).
Read the ABG — acute vs chronic vs acute-on-chronic In respiratory acidosis the kidney compensates by retaining bicarbonate, but at different rates:
  • Acute respiratory acidosis → HCO₃⁻ rises ~1 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg the PaCO₂ climbs above 40.
  • Chronic (compensated) → HCO₃⁻ rises ~4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg above 40 (renal compensation takes days).
  • Acute-on-chronic → the measured bicarbonate sits between the acute and chronic predictions — a decompensated chronic retainer, the classic exacerbation gas.
The A–a gradient is normal in pure hypoventilation but widened in COPD because V/Q mismatch is contributing.
VBG shortcut: venous pH tracks arterial closely (within ~0.03–0.04), and a venous PaCO₂ <45 mmHg reliably rules out arterial hypercarbia — but venous CO₂ can't quantify the degree of retention, so confirm with an ABG when it matters.
📉

The obstructive flow–volume loop

Spirometry is a chronic-phase test, not an acute-exacerbation one — but the obstructive loop explains why exhalation is the problem. The expiratory limb "scoops out" (coved) because floppy, poorly-tethered airways collapse under expiratory pressure, throttling flow.

Normal (blue) vs COPD (red): the coved expiratory limb and reduced peak flow are the signature of airflow limitation. Diagnosis needs post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70.

Comorbidities & drug cautions

🔗

How the usual companions change the course & the plan

ComorbidityHow it changes the exacerbationWhat it changes in management
Cardiovascular disease / IHDLeading cause of death in COPD; exacerbations transiently raise MI/stroke risk. β-agonists + hypoxemia stress the heart.Keep cardioselective β-blockers (they reduce mortality and are safe in COPD); check troponin/ECG; don't withhold needed bronchodilators.
Heart failureOverlaps and mimics — both cause dyspnea, both worsen together.Use BNP + exam ± ultrasound to apportion; diurese the cardiac component; a high pretest for either warrants treating both.
Pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonaleChronic hypoxic vasoconstriction → RV strain, edema, worse hypoxemia during exacerbations.Correct hypoxemia (target 88–92%), gentle diuresis for volume overload; avoid over-diuresis (preload-dependent RV).
DiabetesSystemic steroids cause hyperglycemia; infection worsens control.Monitor glucose q6h while on prednisone; add/uptitrate insulin sliding scale; keep the course short (5 days).
OsteoporosisRepeated steroid courses + smoking + inactivity accelerate bone loss.Minimize cumulative steroid; ensure calcium/vitamin D, DEXA, and bisphosphonate where indicated.
Anxiety / depressionVery common; amplifies dyspnea perception and drives readmission.Pulmonary rehab, SSRIs; be cautious with sedatives (see below).
OSA (overlap syndrome)Combined nocturnal hypoventilation → worse hypercapnia & pulmonary hypertension.Nocturnal NIV/CPAP; screen and treat OSA.
GERDIndependent risk factor for exacerbations (microaspiration).Treat reflux; consider it in the frequent exacerbator.
Lung cancerShares smoking risk; a new mass may masquerade as a "persistent exacerbation".Follow up any suspicious CXR/CT; low-dose CT screening in eligible smokers.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in COPD:
  • Non-selective β-blockers (propranolol, carvedilol in the acutely bronchospastic) — can provoke bronchoconstriction. Use cardioselective agents (metoprolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) instead — they are beneficial and should not be stopped.
  • Benzodiazepines & opioids — respiratory-depressant; can precipitate hypercapnia and arrest in a CO₂-retaining patient. (Exception: low-dose opioids are appropriate for refractory dyspnea in a palliative context.)
  • Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen — over-oxygenation blunts hypoxic drive, worsens V/Q matching (Haldane effect) and dead-space → CO₂ narcosis. Titrate to SpO₂ 88–92%.
  • Excessive/indiscriminate sedation and, when possible, avoid non-essential drugs that dry secretions to the point of mucus plugging in a patient who can't clear them.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient recognition, chronic control & prevention
Assess

When to suspect & who's at risk

🔍

Outpatient presentation

A known-COPD patient reports a sustained change from baseline over hours–days: more breathless, coughing more, more or discoloured sputum, needing their rescue inhaler more often. The single strongest predictor of a future exacerbation is a prior exacerbation — ask every visit.

  • Highest-risk phenotype: ≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalization in the past year (GOLD group E), FEV₁ <50%, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, or persistent eosinophilia.
  • Mimics to keep in mind: pneumonia, heart failure, PE, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, ACS — a "COPD flare" that doesn't add up deserves a CXR, ECG, BNP and a PE thought.
Give every at-risk patient a written COPD action plan plus a "rescue pack" (a short course of prednisone + an antibiotic to start at home on defined criteria) — it shortens recovery and cuts admissions in selected, educated patients.

Chronic management — prevent the next one

💊

Inhaler ladder — first-line → escalation (GOLD 2025)

Long-acting bronchodilators keep the airways splinted open every day so triggers have less room to tip the patient over. ICS adds anti-inflammatory cover only where eosinophilic inflammation is present — otherwise it just raises pneumonia risk without benefit.

1
First-line maintenance — dual LABA + LAMA
Anchor for symptomatic (group B) and exacerbating (group E) patients.
▾

GOLD 2025 favours starting LABA + LAMA (ideally a single inhaler) for most symptomatic patients — superior to monotherapy for symptoms and exacerbations (FLAME trial).

Drug (class)StartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Tiotropium (LAMA)18 µg DPI 1 cap daily or 2.5 µg Respimat 2 puffs dailyOnce-daily — no up-titrationSame (ceiling dose)Blocks M3 muscarinic bronchoconstriction 24 h; best single agent for exacerbation reduction (UPLIFT)Umeclidinium, glycopyrronium, aclidinium (BID)
Olodaterol / formoterol / salmeterol (LABA)Olodaterol 2 puffs daily; formoterol 12 µg BID; salmeterol 50 µg BIDFixed dosingFixedβ₂-agonist relaxes airway smooth muscle for 12–24 hIndacaterol daily; switch within class for tremor/palpitations
LABA/LAMA combosUmeclidinium/vilanterol daily; tiotropium/olodaterol daily; glycopyrronium/formoterol or indacaterolSingle-inhaler, once/twice dailyFixedTwo complementary bronchodilator mechanisms, one device → better adherenceSeparate inhalers if combo unavailable
2
Escalate to triple therapy — add ICS (eosinophil-guided)
For continued exacerbations on LABA/LAMA.
▾

If a patient keeps exacerbating on LABA/LAMA, add an ICS → triple therapy (LABA/LAMA/ICS), guided by the blood eosinophil count:

Blood eosinophilsICS decision (GOLD 2025)
≥ 300 cells/µLStrongly favours ICS — can go directly to triple therapy at diagnosis if exacerbating
100–299 cells/µLConsider ICS if still exacerbating
< 100 cells/µLICS unlikely to help — avoid (pneumonia risk without benefit)

Single-inhaler triple therapy (e.g. fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol daily; budesonide/glycopyrronium/formoterol BID) reduced exacerbations and, in IMPACT and ETHOS, all-cause mortality versus dual therapy in the right patients.

ICS raises pneumonia risk — deprescribe it if eosinophils are low and the patient isn't exacerbating. Never use ICS monotherapy in COPD.

Refractory — add-on agents & biologics
Still exacerbating on optimal triple therapy.
▾
AgentStart → targetWho / whyWatch
Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor)250 µg daily × 4 wk → 500 µg dailyChronic bronchitis + FEV₁ <50% + frequent exacerbations; anti-inflammatoryWeight loss, nausea, diarrhea, mood change
Azithromycin (macrolide)250 mg daily or 500 mg 3×/weekFrequent exacerbators (esp. ex-/non-smokers) — fewer exacerbations (Albert, NEJM 2011)QT prolongation, hearing loss, macrolide resistance — get baseline ECG & audiogram
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα)300 mg SC q2 weeksAdd-on for eosinophilic COPD (eos ≥300) with chronic bronchitis still exacerbating on triple therapy — BOREAS/NOTUS cut exacerbations ~30%Injection-site reaction; specialist-initiated
🚭

The two interventions that change the disease — smoking cessation & rehab

Smoking cessation is the only intervention proven to slow FEV₁ decline and reduce mortality. Combine counselling with pharmacotherapy:

AidStart → targetWhy it worksCautions / alt
Varenicline0.5 mg daily ×3 d → 0.5 mg BID ×4 d → 1 mg BID ×12 wkα4β2 nicotinic partial agonist — blunts cravings & reward; most effective single agentNausea, vivid dreams; take with food
Bupropion SR150 mg daily ×3 d → 150 mg BID; start 1–2 wk before quit dateDopamine/norepi reuptake inhibition reduces cravingsLowers seizure threshold — avoid in seizure/eating disorders
Nicotine replacement (combo)Patch 21 mg/24 h (if ≥10 cig/day) + PRN gum/lozenge 2–4 mgReplaces nicotine, tapered; combo (long + short acting) beats monotherapyLocal skin/oral irritation; safe in stable CVD

Pulmonary rehabilitation after an exacerbation reduces readmissions and improves dyspnea, exercise tolerance and quality of life — refer at discharge. Long-term oxygen therapy (≥15 h/day) improves survival only in chronic severe resting hypoxemia (PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg, or ≤59 with cor pulmonale/polycythemia).

Monitor

Follow-up & titration

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Post-exacerbation visit within 1–4 weeks ("early follow-up") — reassess symptoms, inhaler technique, adherence, and check for a treatable cause of the flare.
  • Inhaler technique every visit — up to 2/3 of patients use their device wrong; a mistimed puff is a wasted drug.
  • Spirometry at diagnosis and periodically (e.g. annually) to track decline.
  • Eosinophils to reassess ICS need; SpO₂ for LTOT eligibility; review the action plan and vaccination status.
  • Escalate inhalers only after confirming adherence + technique — most "treatment failures" are really delivery failures.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & vaccines

🛡️

Grade A & B interventions for this population

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AAsk about tobacco use & provide cessation interventions (behavioural + pharmacotherapy)All adults
BLow-dose CT lung-cancer screening annuallyAdults 50–80 y, ≥20 pack-years, currently smoke or quit ≤15 y
BOne-time AAA screening ultrasoundMen 65–75 y who ever smoked
BStatin for primary CVD prevention (per risk)Adults 40–75 y with ≥1 risk factor & 10-y CVD risk ≥7.5–10%

Note: USPSTF does not recommend screening spirometry in asymptomatic adults (Grade D) — test symptomatic patients.

Vaccinations (CDC/ACIP + GOLD) — every COPD patient

  • Influenza — annually (reduces exacerbations and mortality).
  • Pneumococcal — PCV20 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23.
  • COVID-19 — per current schedule.
  • RSV — adults ≥60 y (and ≥50 with risk) per ACIP.
  • Tdap once, then Td/Tdap booster q10y; zoster ≥50 y.
Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

Red flags — don't manage this in clinic

Refer/admit for: severe dyspnea at rest or unable to speak in full sentences, SpO₂ <90% (or a drop from baseline), new confusion, drowsiness or cyanosis, use of accessory muscles/paradoxical breathing, failure to respond to initial outpatient bronchodilator + steroid, new peripheral edema/cor pulmonale, hemodynamic instability or arrhythmia, inadequate home support, or serious comorbidity (pneumonia, heart failure, PE, new arrhythmia).

🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria (GOLD)

  • Severe symptoms — sudden worsening of resting dyspnea, high RR, falling SpO₂, confusion, drowsiness.
  • Acute respiratory failure (any hypoxemia needing O₂, or hypercapnia).
  • New physical signs — cyanosis, peripheral edema (cor pulmonale).
  • Failure of initial/outpatient management.
  • Serious comorbidities (heart failure, new arrhythmia, pneumonia, PE).
  • Insufficient home support.
Calculate a DECAF score on admission (below) to prognosticate and steer disposition — a validated, COPD-specific mortality tool.

Score

DECAF — in-hospital mortality

🧮

DECAF score calculator

The DECAF score (Steer, Thorax 2012) predicts in-hospital mortality in an acute COPD exacerbation. Tap each item that applies.

Dyspnea (extended MRC, pick one)
eMRCD 1–4 or 5a not applicable 0
eMRCD 5a — too breathless to leave home, independent self-care +1
eMRCD 5b — too breathless & needs help washing/dressing +2
Other predictors
Eosinopenia (<0.05 ×10⁹/L) +1
Consolidation on CXR +1
Acidemia (pH <7.30) +1
Atrial fibrillation (ECG or history) +1
0
DECAF 0–1 = low risk (in-hospital mortality ~1.4%) → consider early supported discharge; DECAF 3–6 = high risk (~34%) → escalate monitoring, early senior/ICU input, and address goals of care. Mortality bands from Steer 2012 (derivation cohort).

💊

Anthonisen — should I give antibiotics?

Tap the cardinal symptoms present. Antibiotics benefit exacerbations with increased sputum purulence (Anthonisen type 1, or type 2 with purulence) — or any patient needing mechanical ventilation.

① Increased dyspnea
② Increased sputum volume
③ Increased sputum purulence
On mechanical ventilation (NIV or invasive)
—
Select the symptoms present.
First-line for an uncomplicated case: azithromycin, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5–7 days. Escalate to a respiratory fluoroquinolone / anti-pseudomonal β-lactam for resistance or Pseudomonas risk (severe COPD, bronchiectasis, recent abx/hospitalization).

🔗

Other validated scores — use MDCalc for the exact math

These use continuous variables or cohort-derived class tables; rather than re-implement (and risk mis-scoring), compute them on MDCalc:

  • BAP-65 — BUN ≥25, Altered mental status, Pulse ≥109, age ≥65; stratifies mortality & mechanical-ventilation need in AECOPD. MDCalc
  • CURB-65 — if pneumonia coexists, for severity/disposition. MDCalc
  • CAT (COPD Assessment Test) & mMRC dyspnea — for chronic symptom burden / ABE grouping. CAT · mMRC
  • BODE index — long-term mortality prognostic (BMI, Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise). MDCalc

Treat

Acute management — the bundle

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy — doses & ladders

1
Bronchodilators — SABA + SAMA, scheduled
Open the airways; the fastest symptom relief.
▾
β₂-agonists relax airway smooth muscle within minutes; short-acting antimuscarinics block vagal bronchoconstriction and dry secretions. Combining the two mechanisms beats either alone.

DrugStartTitrationMax / notesWhy / monitor
Albuterol (SABA)2.5 mg nebulized q1h ×3 then q2–4h; or MDI 4–8 puffs q1–4h with spacerSpace out as improvingMDI-with-spacer ≈ nebulizer efficacy; q1h in severe distressTremor, tachycardia, ↓K⁺ — recheck K⁺
Ipratropium (SAMA)0.5 mg nebulized q4h; or MDI 2 puffs q4hScheduled q4–6hOften combined with albuterol (DuoNeb)Dry mouth, urinary retention, avoid in eye if glaucoma spray

Resume/continue the patient's long-acting inhalers during admission and confirm technique before discharge.

2
Systemic corticosteroids — short course
Damp the airway inflammation driving the flare.
▾
Steroids switch off transcription of inflammatory cytokines, shrinking mucosal edema over 24–48 h. They speed recovery, improve FEV₁ and oxygenation, and cut treatment failure and length of stay.

DrugDoseDurationWhy / evidenceMonitor
Prednisone (PO)40 mg PO once daily5 days (no taper needed)REDUCE trial (Leuppi, JAMA 2013): 5 days = 14 days, less steroid exposureHyperglycemia, insomnia, mood, HTN; check glucose q6h
Methylprednisolone (IV)40–60 mg IV daily (≈ prednisone 40)5 days, switch to PO when toleratingFor those who can't take PO or are critically illSame as above; no benefit to higher doses
Longer courses and IV routes carry more harm without more benefit in most patients — 5 days, oral, 40 mg is the default. Nebulized budesonide is a steroid-sparing alternative in selected patients who tolerate systemic steroids poorly.

3
Antibiotics — when purulence or severity says bacterial
Anthonisen-guided, not automatic.
▾

Indications: ≥2 cardinal symptoms with increased sputum purulence (Anthonisen type 1, or type 2 with purulence), or any exacerbation requiring mechanical ventilation (NIV or invasive). Duration 5–7 days.

ScenarioAgent & doseWhyAlt / caution
UncomplicatedAzithromycin 500 mg ×1 then 250 mg daily ×4 d; or doxycycline 100 mg BID; or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg BIDCover H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalisMacrolide → QT; doxy in pregnancy caution
Risk factors / prior resistanceAmoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg BID; or respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 500–750 mg daily)Broader Gram-negative coverFQ: tendinopathy, QT, dysglycemia, C. diff
Pseudomonas risk (severe COPD, bronchiectasis, recent abx/hospitalization)Levofloxacin 750 mg daily; or anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime) — culture-directedCover P. aeruginosaDe-escalate on cultures
A low procalcitonin can support holding or stopping antibiotics, but GOLD advises caution — sputum purulence and the Anthonisen count remain the primary triggers.

4
Controlled oxygen — target 88–92%
Enough to correct hypoxemia; not so much you cause CO₂ narcosis.
▾
In a CO₂ retainer, high-flow O₂ worsens V/Q matching (releasing hypoxic vasoconstriction), the Haldane effect and dead-space → the PaCO₂ climbs and the pH falls. Titrated O₂ corrects hypoxemia while preserving respiratory drive.

  • Target SpO₂ 88–92% — deliver by Venturi mask (precise FiO₂ 24–28%) or nasal cannula 1–2 L/min, titrated.
  • Recheck an ABG within 30–60 min of starting/changing O₂ to catch a rising PaCO₂.
  • Austin (BMJ 2010): titrated O₂ (88–92%) roughly halved pre-hospital mortality vs high-flow 100% O₂ in suspected COPD.
5
Adjuncts & what NOT to do
Rounding out the bundle.
▾
  • VTE prophylaxis, glucose management on steroids, electrolyte repletion (K⁺, Mg²⁺ — β-agonists drop K⁺).
  • Methylxanthines (theophylline/aminophylline): not recommended — narrow therapeutic window, arrhythmias, minimal benefit.
  • Chest physiotherapy / routine mucolytics: no clear acute benefit; airway clearance selectively if secretion-limited.
  • Treat the trigger and comorbidity (HF, arrhythmia, PE) you find on work-up.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Respiratory: RR, work of breathing, SpO₂ on the lowest FiO₂ that holds 88–92%, breath sounds/air movement. Repeat ABG if distress or drowsiness worsens.
  • Wean nebs to the home inhaler as the patient improves — space albuterol from q1–2h to q4–6h.
  • Glucose (steroid hyperglycemia), K⁺/Mg²⁺, mental status (early CO₂ narcosis).
  • Mobility & secretions — get them up early; assess swallow if fatigued.
  • Confirm the discharge bundle is coming together: inhaler technique, action plan, rehab referral, follow-up booked, vaccines updated, smoking cessation started.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU / high-dependency for any of:
  • Respiratory acidosis with pH < 7.35 (esp. <7.30) and PaCO₂ > 45–60 not improving on ward NIV.
  • Persistent/worsening hypoxemia (PaO₂ < 40 mmHg) or need for FiO₂ that can't maintain SpO₂ ≥88%.
  • Failure of NIV (worsening pH/PaCO₂, intolerance, or altered mental status).
  • Hemodynamic instability / need for vasopressors; life-threatening arrhythmia.
  • Decreasing consciousness, exhaustion, or impending respiratory arrest → intubation.

Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness (GOLD): needs short-acting bronchodilator no more often than every 4 h; able to walk across the room; able to eat and sleep without frequent waking from dyspnea; clinically and gas-exchange stable for 12–24 h; able (or arranged) to use inhalers; follow-up and home care arranged; patient/family/physician confident in home management.

Home

Back to baseline function, stable gases, reliable inhaler use & support.

Home health

Home + nursing/respiratory visits, home O₂ setup & teaching.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing / deconditioned, <3 h therapy/day tolerable.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines — pulmonary rehab candidate.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care — e.g. slow ventilator/NIV weaning >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Advanced COPD, recurrent failure, refractory dyspnea; goals-focused care.
Book an early (1–4 week) follow-up and refer to pulmonary rehab at discharge — both cut readmissions. A discharge that skips inhaler-technique teaching is a bounce-back waiting to happen.

🫁 ICU — respiratory failure & ventilatory support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

GOLD indications for ICU admission:

  • Severe dyspnea responding inadequately to initial emergency therapy.
  • Changes in mental status (confusion, lethargy, coma).
  • Persistent/worsening hypoxemia (PaO₂ < 40 mmHg) and/or severe/worsening respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.25) despite supplemental O₂ and NIV.
  • Need for invasive mechanical ventilation.
  • Hemodynamic instability — need for vasopressors.
A silent chest, paradoxical (abdominal) breathing, bradycardia, or a falling RR in a tiring patient signals impending respiratory arrest — prepare to intubate now, don't wait for the next gas.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Serial ABGs — the pH/PaCO₂ trajectory over the first 1–2 h on NIV is the best predictor of success or failure.
  • Continuous SpO₂ + capnography (EtCO₂ trend); telemetry for AF/MAT.
  • Arterial line if frequent gases or hemodynamic instability; central access if vasopressors.
  • Target SpO₂ 88–92%; correct the pH toward normal, not overshoot; watch K⁺/Mg²⁺/glucose.
Support

NIV — the single biggest intervention

😷

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) & high-flow O₂

BiPAP delivers a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) that augments each breath — unloading fatigued respiratory muscles and boosting alveolar ventilation to blow off CO₂ — plus a lower expiratory pressure (EPAP) that splints airways and offsets auto-PEEP, cutting the work of triggering a breath.

Start NIV early in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure — pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg — and/or severe dyspnea with accessory-muscle use/paradoxical breathing. NIV reduces intubation, mortality and length of stay (Brochard NEJM 1995; Plant Lancet 2000).

IPAP (start)
8–12 cmH₂O
titrate up ~2 q10–20 min to relieve dyspnea & ↓CO₂ (to ~20)
EPAP (start)
4–5 cmH₂O
offsets auto-PEEP, improves triggering

Contraindications to NIVPredictors of NIV failure
Respiratory arrest / need to intubate now; reduced consciousness unable to protect airway; hemodynamic instability; facial trauma/surgery; high aspiration risk; copious secretions; uncooperative patientpH <7.25 at start or not improving after 1–2 h; rising PaCO₂; worsening mental status; asynchrony/intolerance; severe acidosis with tachypnea

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is an option for hypoxemic patients who don't tolerate NIV or between NIV sessions; it provides some CO₂ washout and low-level PEEP but is not first-line for hypercapnic acidosis — NIV is.

Reassess at 1–2 h: improving pH/PaCO₂ and comfort → continue and wean. Failing (pH still <7.25, worsening CO₂, deteriorating mental status) → intubate — don't let a tiring patient languish on a failing mask.

Airway

Invasive ventilation — obstructive settings

🌬️

When NIV fails — the vent for air trapping

Indications for intubation: NIV failure or contraindication, respiratory or cardiac arrest, apnea/gasping, decreased consciousness unable to protect airway, massive aspiration/secretions, severe hemodynamic instability, life-threatening hypoxemia.

The enemy in obstructive physiology is breath-stacking / auto-PEEP: if you don't allow enough time to exhale, air accumulates, intrathoracic pressure rises, venous return drops → hypotension and barotrauma. The whole ventilator strategy is built around maximizing expiratory time.

Mode
Volume A/C
predictable minute ventilation
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective
Resp rate
low: 10–12
longer expiratory time
I:E ratio
1:3 – 1:4
prolong expiration (↑ inspiratory flow)
Plateau pressure
< 30 cmH₂O
limit barotrauma
Strategy
Permissive hypercapnia
tolerate ↑CO₂ / pH ≥7.15–7.20

Measuring & managing auto-PEEP: quantify it with an end-expiratory hold; aim to keep it < ~10 cmH₂O. Set extrinsic PEEP at roughly 70–80% of the measured intrinsic PEEP — this lowers the inspiratory threshold the patient must overcome to trigger, reducing work and dyssynchrony without adding to hyperinflation.

Sudden hypotension or a rising plateau pressure on the vent → think dynamic hyperinflation or pneumothorax. Disconnect the circuit and let the chest fully deflate (a "vent holiday"); if it doesn't fix quickly, decompress a suspected tension pneumothorax.

Adequate sedation ± short-term paralysis may be needed to prevent asynchrony/breath-stacking. Vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) are for genuine shock — most COPD hypotension after intubation is auto-PEEP/sedation, so treat the trapping and give fluid before chasing pressors.

Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When the vent isn't enough

  • ECCO₂R / veno-venous ECMO — extracorporeal CO₂ removal or ECMO as a bridge in refractory, severe hypercapnic acidosis at experienced centres; still investigational for routine use.
  • Aggressive bronchodilation — continuous nebulized β-agonist; consider IV magnesium (2 g) as an adjunct for refractory bronchospasm (stronger evidence in asthma).
  • Rule out and treat complications driving the failure: pneumothorax, PE, pneumonia, mucus plugging (bronchoscopy for lobar collapse), heart failure.
  • Goals of care — advanced COPD with recurrent ventilatory failure warrants an early, explicit conversation about intubation preferences and palliative options.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: pH normalized and PaCO₂ back toward the patient's baseline, off NIV (or on stable nocturnal-only settings) or successfully extubated, SpO₂ ≥88–92% on low-flow O₂, hemodynamically stable off/weaning vasopressors, mental status at baseline, and short-acting bronchodilator need > every 2–4 h.
Not yet if: still requiring frequent NIV for acidosis, escalating O₂/FiO₂, labile hemodynamics, or fluctuating mental status.

Prolonged failure to wean → consider tracheostomy and LTAC for slow ventilator liberation, and revisit goals of care.

Shared

Clinical pearls

💡

The high-yield takeaways

  1. Target SpO₂ 88–92%, not higher. Titrated O₂ roughly halved mortality vs high-flow (Austin 2010). The mechanism of O₂-induced hypercapnia is mainly loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → V/Q mismatch (Haldane effect ~25%); the old "you'll knock out their hypoxic drive" story is the smallest contributor.
  2. NIV is the single highest-yield intervention in acute hypercapnic failure (pH <7.35, PaCO₂ >45) — it cuts intubation and mortality. Reassess at 1–2 h; no improvement is the strongest predictor of NIV failure and the cue to intubate.
  3. Five days of prednisone 40 mg is enough (REDUCE) — equal to 14 days with less steroid exposure; no taper needed.
  4. Sputum purulence is the key antibiotic trigger — a colour change beats sputum volume for predicting a bacterial cause.
  5. Blood eosinophils steer inhaled steroids: ≥300 favours ICS/triple therapy and dupilumab; <100 argues against ICS (pneumonia risk without benefit).
  6. On the vent, the enemy is auto-PEEP — give time to exhale (low RR, I:E 1:3–1:4, permissive hypercapnia, Pplat <30). Sudden hypotension after intubation → disconnect and let the chest deflate.
  7. Cardioselective β-blockers are safe and beneficial in COPD with CAD/HF (metoprolol, bisoprolol) — don't withhold them; only non-selective agents risk bronchospasm.
  8. Don't reflexively CXR every flare — it's abnormal in ~14–16% and changes management in only ~4.5%. Image when you suspect pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion or CHF.
  9. Consider PE in an exacerbation with no clear infective trigger — an under-recognized mimic; low threshold for CTPA.
  10. A VBG triages, an ABG decides: venous pH tracks arterial closely and a venous PaCO₂ <45 rules out hypercarbia, but venous CO₂ can't quantify retention.
  11. MDI + spacer = nebulizer for bronchodilator delivery (Cochrane) — handy for cost and aerosol reduction.
  12. Prevention beats rescue: smoking cessation, vaccination, O₂ for chronic hypoxemia and NIV are the interventions with mortality benefit; refer to pulmonary rehab within ~4 weeks of discharge to cut readmissions.
  13. Low-dose opioids relieve refractory dyspnea in advanced/palliative COPD when carefully titrated — a deliberate exception to the general caution against respiratory depressants.
